newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU must end farm export subsidies, Fischler says.
newsitem.headline: EU must end farm export subsidies, Fischler says.

text.p: The European Union, the world's biggest agricultural producer, must learn to export without the aid of subsidies if it is to share in expanding world markets, EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler said on Monday.

"In the long run, this will only be possible if we continue to wean exports away from export subsidies," Fischler told a conference organised by the European Parliament's Land Use and Food Policy Intergroup.
But the EU is currently taxing wheat exports as a precautionary move to prevent prices overheating and ensure adequate supplies for domestic consumers.
Fischler told reporters afterwards that the tax would be kept for the moment because world prices remain high.
Fischler reiterated that new reforms will be needed, notably in the cereals and beef sectors, to prevent surpluses recurring early next century.
He warned there was also a serious risk of new dairy, olive oil and wine surpluses developing.
Fischler doubted whether tighter production curbs, such as increased set-aside or new production quotas, were the solution.

If farm policy remains unchanged, cereals set-aside would have to be raised to between 23 and 25 percent after 2002 when central and east European countries start to join the EU, he told reporters afterwards.
"It's not something farmers will accept, especially young farmers," he said.
Fischler said in his speech that the EU will rely less and less on price support mechanisms, such as intervention, because it cannot guarantee farm incomes in the long term.
"In markets where competitiveness will become even more important in the future, a route involving artificially high prices will quickly lead to a dead-end," he said.
EU market and income policies will become increasingly separated, he added.

"This is an approach which I believe has considerable advantages," he said, adding that payments to compensate farmers for income losses caused by cuts in support prices and set-aside curbs, should form the basis of future reforms.
Looking ahead to World Trade Organisation (WTO) farm talks starting in 1999, Fischler warned that the EU will be pressed to make further cuts in subsidies and open its markets to imports.
"We have to analyse the consequences now, if we want to avoid the Union having to negotiate with its back to the wall," he said.
But simply liberalising markets does not solve all the problems, he said, adding however that EU agriculture must be competitive and that the right conditions must be provided.
